form-field.what: A form field pairs one input with its label, hint and error message. It is the basic unit people fill in to give information.
uses: Collecting a name, email address or number in a sign-up or settings form.
Picking one option from a dropdown inside a form.
Entering longer text, such as a message or description.
avoid: For a single yes or no choice, use a checkbox or switch instead.
For a short list of options, use radio buttons so all choices stay visible.
practices: Put a visible label above every input; never rely on placeholder text alone.
Show the hint before the input and the error next to it.
Say what is wrong and how to fix it in error messages.
Mark optional fields rather than required ones when most fields are required.
Use the right input type so phones show a suitable keyboard.

toggle-field.what: A single checkbox or switch with its label and description. It lets people turn one option on or off.
uses: Agreeing to terms or opting in to emails.
Turning a feature on or off in settings.
Marking one yes or no answer inside a longer form.
avoid: For picking one answer from several, use radio buttons instead.
For a choice that needs a Save button, use a checkbox rather than an instant switch.
practices: Word the label as the result of turning it on, in positive terms.
Use a switch only when the change takes effect immediately.
Make the whole label clickable, not just the small box.
Keep descriptions short and place them under the label.
Show an error next to the control if a required box is left unticked.

choice-group.what: A set of radio buttons or checkboxes under one question. Radios allow one answer; checkboxes allow several.
uses: Choosing a plan, delivery method or frequency from a few options.
Selecting several interests or notification channels.
Answering a survey question with a short list of answers.
avoid: For a long list of options, use a dropdown or searchable picker instead.
For one on or off setting, use a single checkbox or switch.
practices: Wrap the options in a fieldset with a legend that states the question.
Keep the list short, usually 2 to 7 options for radios.
Order options in a logical way, not at random.
Pre-select a safe default only when most people would choose it.
Show an error message for the whole group, not each option.

search-field.what: A text box for typing a few words to narrow down what is already on the page, with a clear button and a result count.
uses: Filtering a table, list or menu as the person types.
Finding one item in a long settings or help list.
Narrowing results on a page without reloading it.
avoid: For searching a whole site or large collection, use a full search form with a button.
For a short list of 5 or fewer items, no search is needed.
practices: Label the field clearly, even when the label is visually hidden.
Show the number of results and update it as people type.
Provide a clear button to reset the filter in one click.
Wait a moment after typing stops before filtering heavy lists.
Show a helpful message when nothing matches.

search-bar.what: A search form with a text box and a button, sometimes with a menu to limit the search area. People submit it to see results.
uses: Searching a whole website, shop or knowledge base.
Finding records in a large database or archive.
Searching within one category chosen from a menu.
avoid: To narrow a list already on screen, use an instant filter field instead.
For a few items, browsing or a menu is quicker than searching.
practices: Place it where people expect it, usually the top of the page.
Support the Enter key as well as the button.
Keep the typed query visible on the results page.
Put the query in the web address so results can be shared.
Offer help when there are no results, such as spelling tips.

table-toolbar.what: A row of controls above a table or list that holds search, filters, view options and actions, plus bulk actions for selected rows.
uses: Searching and filtering a large data table.
Applying one action to many selected rows at once.
Exporting or adding records from a list page.
avoid: For short lists with no actions, a toolbar adds clutter; leave it out.
For actions on a single row, use a row menu instead.
practices: Group controls by purpose: finding on the left, acting on the right.
Show the number of selected rows next to the bulk actions.
Hide actions that do not apply to the current selection.
Keep the toolbar in one row on wide screens and wrap it cleanly on small ones.
Give the toolbar a label so screen readers can announce it.

multi-picker.what: A dropdown that lets people filter a long list and tick several items. The chosen items appear as tags that can be removed.
uses: Assigning several people or teams to a task.
Choosing multiple categories or tags for an item.
Selecting several sites, devices or products from a long list.
avoid: For a short list that fits on screen, use a checkbox group instead.
For picking only one item, use a select or searchable dropdown.
practices: Add a filter box when the list has more than about 10 items.
Show chosen items as removable tags so they stay visible.
Summarize the selection in the button, such as the number chosen.
Provide Clear and Done buttons inside the list.
Make every option reachable and selectable by keyboard.

language-switcher.what: A control that lets people change the language of a site or app. Each language is shown in its own name.
uses: Letting visitors switch a site between supported languages.
Setting the interface language in an account menu.
Offering translations in a footer of a public website.
avoid: Do not guess language from location alone; offer a choice as well.
For a site in one language, leave the switcher out.
practices: Write each language in its own language, such as Deutsch or Français.
Do not use flags, since one flag does not stand for one language.
Place it in a predictable spot, such as the header or footer.
Keep the person on the same page after switching.
Mark each option with its language code so screen readers read it correctly.

input-group.what: A text input joined to a fixed piece of text or a button, such as a unit, a currency sign or an action like Copy.
uses: Entering an amount next to a currency or a unit like days or kg.
Typing a web address with a fixed prefix.
Adding a Copy or Test button right beside a value.
avoid: For several unrelated actions, use separate buttons outside the field.
For plain values with no unit, a normal input is enough.
practices: Show the unit or prefix beside the value so people do not guess.
Keep the attached text short.
Link the addon to the input so screen readers read both.
Use a button only for an action that directly relates to the input.
Make sure the group stays readable on narrow screens.

filter-button.what: A button that opens a panel of filters and shows how many are active. It keeps the page simple until filters are needed.
uses: Narrowing a product or record list by many attributes.
Showing advanced filters that do not fit in a toolbar.
Telling people at a glance that a list is already filtered.
avoid: For one or two simple filters, show them directly instead of hiding them.
For free-text narrowing, use a search field.
practices: Show the number of active filters on the button.
Show active filters as removable tags outside the panel.
Offer a clear all option.
Tell the person how many results the filters give.
Announce the open or closed state to assistive technology.

dropdown-select.what: A button that opens a list of options, where each option can include a short description or icon.
uses: Choosing a role and seeing what each role can do.
Picking a plan with a line explaining its limits.
Selecting an option that needs a second line to tell it apart.
avoid: When options are plain words, use the native select; it works better everywhere.
When people must compare choices side by side, use radio buttons.
practices: Keep the list to a manageable length, often 5 to 15 options.
Show the current choice on the button.
Support arrow keys, Enter and Escape.
Return focus to the button when the list closes.
Keep descriptions short and written in plain words.

combobox.what: A text box that suggests matching options as people type. The final value must be one of the suggestions.
uses: Choosing a country, city or person from a long list.
Finding a product or record by typing part of its name.
Selecting an item when people know its name already.
avoid: For short lists of about 15 items or fewer, use a normal select.
When any text is allowed, use a plain input with optional suggestions.
practices: Start suggesting after one or two typed letters.
Highlight the part of each suggestion that matches the typed text.
Show no more than about 10 suggestions at a time.
Support arrow keys, Enter and Escape.
Show a clear message when nothing matches.

auto-suggest.what: A free text box that offers common answers from a list while still allowing anything to be typed.
uses: Entering a tag, department or location where many answers repeat.
Speeding up typing of common values without limiting them.
Entering a job title or company name.
avoid: When the answer must be from a fixed list, use a combobox or select.
For answers that are always different, plain input is simpler.
practices: Put the most common suggestions first.
Keep the list reasonably short.
Do not block answers that are not in the list.
Still label the field clearly.
Check typed values on the server, just as for any input.

otp-input.what: A set of boxes for typing a one-time code, such as a six-digit number sent by text or email to confirm identity.
uses: Confirming a login with two-step verification.
Verifying a phone number or email address.
Approving a sensitive action such as a payment.
avoid: For long passwords, use a password field; codes are meant to be short and single-use.
Do not use codes where a simpler check would do.
practices: Tell people where the code was sent and how long it lasts.
Allow pasting the whole code and browser autofill.
Offer a Send a new code option after a short wait.
Show errors that say whether the code was wrong or expired.
Use a numeric keypad on phones.

rating-input.what: A row of stars people select to give a score, usually from 1 to 5. It is a quick way to collect an opinion.
uses: Rating a product, service or support conversation.
Collecting quick feedback after a task.
Letting people review a purchase or place.
avoid: For detailed feedback, add a text box; stars alone say little.
For measuring likelihood to recommend, use a 0 to 10 scale instead.
practices: Show the chosen value in words, such as 4 of 5.
Label each star so screen readers read the number.
Make stars large enough to tap easily.
Let people change their rating before submitting.
Make clear what the lowest and highest ratings mean.

split-date.what: Three separate boxes for day, month and year. People type a date they already know instead of picking it in a calendar.
uses: Entering a birth date.
Entering a document date such as an expiry or issue date.
Any date far in the past or future.
avoid: For dates near today, such as a booking, use a calendar date picker.
For relative dates like next week, offer shortcuts or a picker.
practices: Label each box clearly as Day, Month and Year.
Give an example, such as 27 3 2024.
Order the boxes the way the reader's region writes dates.
Use numeric keypads on phones.
Show one error for the whole date, not three.

file-field.what: An area where people choose or drag files to upload. It lists the chosen files and states what is allowed.
uses: Uploading documents, photos or a profile picture.
Importing data from a spreadsheet file.
Attaching files to a message or request.
avoid: For tiny text, ask people to type it rather than upload a file.
For many large files, use a dedicated uploader with progress and retry.
practices: State accepted file types and the size limit before upload.
Let people click or drag and drop.
Show the chosen file names so they can be checked.
Show progress for large uploads.
Check file type and size again on the server.

form-alert.what: A message at the top of a form that reports a problem not tied to one field, such as a conflict or permission error.
uses: Showing that a save failed because of a server problem.
Warning that chosen dates clash with another record.
Explaining that the person lacks permission to submit.
avoid: For a problem with one field, show the error next to that field.
For good news or neutral tips, use an info or success message.
practices: Place it above the fields so it is seen first.
Say what went wrong and what to do next.
Use an error icon as well as colour.
Announce it to screen readers when it appears.
Add a summary with links when several fields are invalid.

form-actions.what: The row of buttons at the end of a form, with the main action first and others such as Cancel after it.
uses: Saving or submitting a form.
Offering Cancel next to Save in a dialog.
Placing a Delete action away from the main buttons.
avoid: Do not scatter several equal buttons through the form; keep actions together at the end.
For actions that apply instantly, such as switches, no button row is needed.
practices: Make one primary action stand out, labelled with a verb.
Place buttons directly after the last field.
Put destructive actions apart and ask to confirm.
Keep the Cancel option easy to reach.
Stack buttons full width on small screens.

form-section.what: A group of related fields under a heading, with a short note about what the group is for.
uses: Splitting a long settings page into topics.
Grouping billing, contact and account details separately.
Making a long form feel shorter.
avoid: For a short form with a handful of fields, headings only add clutter.
For steps that must happen in order, use a multi-step form.
practices: Give each section a clear, descriptive heading.
Group only fields that belong together.
Add a one-sentence description when the purpose is unclear.
Keep the order logical, with the most important sections first.
Use proper heading levels so screen readers can navigate.

form-stack.what: A layout that arranges form fields in one column, or in two columns when fields are short and closely related.
uses: Laying out almost any form in one clear column.
Placing start and end values side by side.
Fitting many short fields into a compact admin form.
avoid: Do not use many columns for long forms; people skip fields and lose their place.
For unrelated fields, keep one column.
practices: Prefer one column for a single reading path.
Use two columns only for short, related pairs.
Keep consistent spacing between fields.
Limit the line width so inputs are not stretched too wide.
Fall back to one column on phones.

schedule-editor.what: A form control for setting weekly times, built from rows of day, start and end time that can be added or removed.
uses: Setting opening hours for a shop or service.
Defining when a recording or alert is active.
Choosing quiet hours for notifications.
avoid: For a single date and time, use a date and time picker.
For a repeating rule like every second Tuesday, use a recurrence form.
practices: Offer presets such as business hours for common cases.
Let people add and remove rows easily.
Warn when rows overlap as soon as they are entered.
Show a time format people recognise.
Make each row's remove button describe which row it removes.

zone-editor.what: A tool for drawing shapes or lines over an image or map by clicking points, next to a list of the shapes drawn.
uses: Marking areas of interest on a camera image.
Drawing a delivery or coverage area.
Defining regions to include or exclude on a floor plan.
avoid: For choosing from fixed areas, use a list or select instead of drawing.
For precise measurements, offer typed coordinates instead of drawing only.
practices: Offer undo and clear so mistakes cost little.
Show a status line saying what to do next.
Provide typed coordinate fields as an alternative to drawing.
Show a label and colour for each shape.
Store the shapes as simple data the server can check.

login-card.what: The sign-in form: a small panel with logo, email, password, a remember option, a sign-in button and a link to recover access.
uses: Signing people in to an account or application.
Starting a session in an admin area.
Requesting access to a private site.
avoid: For one-click access to a public site, avoid forcing a login.
For sign-up, use a registration form with more fields.
practices: Keep it short: only ask for what is needed to sign in.
Allow browsers and password managers to fill in the fields.
Use a general error message that does not say which field was wrong.
Offer a clear password reset link.
Let people show the password they typed.

properties-editor.what: A list of key and value rows where people add their own details. It suits free-form data without a fixed structure.
uses: Adding custom fields or labels to a record.
Editing HTTP headers or settings pairs.
Storing extra metadata that varies between items.
avoid: For known fields, use normal form fields; they are clearer and easier to validate.
For large structured data, use an import or a dedicated editor.
practices: Provide clear Key and Value labels on every row.
Reject duplicate keys with an error on the repeated row.
Trim extra spaces without bothering the person.
Make Add and Remove buttons easy to find and name.
Keep focus on the new row after adding it.

rich-text-editor.what: A text area with a small toolbar for formatting, such as bold, italic, lists and links. It produces formatted text.
uses: Writing notes, comments or descriptions that need simple formatting.
Composing messages with links and lists.
Editing short content like a product description.
avoid: For plain notes, use a normal text area.
For long documents or code, use a dedicated editor.
practices: Offer only the few formatting options people really need.
Label every toolbar button and show its pressed state.
Support common keyboard shortcuts such as Ctrl+B.
Clean and sanitize the saved HTML on the server.
Keep a plain text fallback when scripts do not run.

product-item.what: A tile in a shop or catalogue that shows a product's picture, name, price and a main action.
uses: Showing items in a shop grid or list.
Listing products in a catalogue or quote tool.
Displaying recommended or related products.
avoid: For detailed comparison of specs, use a table instead of tiles.
For a single product page, use a larger detail layout.
practices: Use a consistent image shape so tiles line up.
Make the product name a link to the details.
Show the current price clearly, with any old price marked as such.
Offer just one main action per tile.
Let long names wrap instead of cutting them off.

person-block.what: A small block that shows a person's picture, name and role, sometimes with a way to contact them.
uses: Showing the owner or assignee of a task.
Listing contacts, team members or authors.
Displaying the author of an article or comment.
avoid: For a long directory of people, use a table with search.
For full profiles, use a profile page or card.
practices: Show the name as the person wrote it.
Add a role or title to give context.
Use initials when there is no photo.
Give contact buttons accurate descriptive names.
Keep the layout consistent wherever people appear.

post-block.what: A short teaser for an article that shows a headline, a few lines of text, details such as date and a small image.
uses: Listing news, blog posts or release notes.
Showing related articles under a post.
Showing help articles in a search result list.
avoid: For one prominent story, use a larger featured layout.
For plain lists of links, a simple text list is enough.
practices: Start with a headline that tells what the article is about.
Keep the excerpt short and cut at a natural point.
Show the date and reading time.
Make the headline the link.
Move the image above the text on small screens.

hero.what: The large opening section of a landing page. It states what the product offers and gives one clear next step.
uses: Opening a home or marketing page.
Introducing a new product or campaign.
Welcoming people at the start of onboarding.
avoid: Do not use it in everyday application screens where people need to get work done.
Do not use several heroes on one page.
practices: State the benefit in a short headline.
Offer one main action and at most one secondary action.
Use an image that supports the message.
Keep the text readable over any background.
Make sure the main action is visible without scrolling.

photo-actions-bar.what: A row of small buttons under a photo, such as like, comment and share, often with counts.
uses: Letting people react to photos in a feed.
Offering share and save in a gallery.
Showing engagement counts under a shared image.
avoid: For one main action on an image, a single button is clearer.
For heavy editing actions, use a toolbar or menu.
practices: Use familiar icons so people know what each does.
Give every icon button a text name for screen readers.
Show a pressed state for toggles such as like.
Show counts beside the related action.
Make buttons big enough to tap.

video-card.what: A card that shows a video's latest picture with its name, status and quick actions.
uses: Showing cameras or recordings in a dashboard grid.
Listing videos in a library.
Monitoring which live feeds are online.
avoid: To compare many videos by data, use a table.
To watch one video in detail, use a full player view.
practices: Show a thumbnail first so people recognise the video.
Mark the status with text as well as colour.
Show when the image was taken.
Make the whole card clickable to open the video.
Show a clear placeholder when no image is available.

story-feature.what: A large featured article block with a big image, headline, intro text and details. It highlights the top story on a page.
uses: Showing the lead story on a news or blog page.
Featuring a case study or announcement.
Highlighting the newest release notes.
avoid: For lists of many stories, use smaller teaser blocks.
Do not feature several stories at once; the highlight is lost.
practices: Use one strong image with a helpful description.
Write a headline that tells the story.
Keep the intro to a few lines.
Show the date and reading time.
Stack image and text on small screens.

factoid.what: A single large number or fact with a short sentence and its source. It makes one result easy to remember.
uses: Highlighting a key result in a report or case study.
Adding a striking statistic to a landing page.
Summarizing one finding in a story.
avoid: For several figures together, use a grid of summary tiles.
For data that needs context over time, use a chart.
practices: Show one number only and make it large.
Explain in a sentence what the number means.
Always give the source and date.
Use a number you can back up.
Keep text readable against the background.
